<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wit|6950|'''wit'''}}</noinclude>(see ''wite''<sup>1</sup>); Teut. √ ''wit'', see, = OBulg. ''vidieti'' = Serv. ''vidjeti'' = Bohem. ''widěti'' = Russ. ''vidietĭ'', see, = L. ''vidēre'', see, = Gr. ἰδεῖν, see (perf. οἶδα, I know, = E. ''wot''), = Skt. √ ''vid'', see, perceive. From the verb ''wit''<sup>1</sup> are ult. E. ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', ''wit''<sup>2</sup>, ''wise''<sup>1</sup>, ''wise''<sup>2</sup> (''guise'', ''disguise''), ''wise''<sup>3</sup>, ''wiss'', ''wisdom'', etc., ''witch'', ''wick''<sup>7</sup>, ''wicked'', ''wiseacre'', ''iwis'', ''wis''<sup>1</sup>, ''wis''<sup>2</sup>, ''witness'', ''witter'', ''witterly'', ''wizard'', etc. (see also ''wite''<sup>1</sup>, ''wite''<sup>2</sup>); from the L. ''vidēre'' are ult. E. ''visage'', ''vision'', ''visit'', ''visual'', etc. (see under ''vision''); from the Gr., ''idea'', ''idol'', ''idolon'', ''eidolon'', etc., and the element ''-eid-'' in ''kaleidoscope'', ''-id'' in the termination ''-oid'', etc.] To know; be or become aware: used with or without an object, the object when present often being a clause or statement. {{smaller|(''a'') Present tense: I ''wot'' (''wote''), thou ''wost'' (erroneously ''wotiest'', ''wotst''), he ''wot'' (erroneously ''wotteth''); plural we, ye (you), they ''wit''. [Archaic.]}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But natheles, yit ''wot'' I wel also
That ther nis noon dwelling in this contree,
That either hath in heven or helle ybe,
Ne may of it non other weyes ''witen'',
But as he hath herd seyd or founde it writen.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thei seyn to hir Womman, what wepist thou? She seid to hem, For thei han takun a wey my lord, and I ''woot'' not where thei have putt him. {{right|''Wyclif'', John xx. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Dead long ygoe, I ''wote'', thou haddest bin.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. ii. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wottest'' thou what I say, man?</poem>
{{right|''The World and the Child'' (O. E. Plays, I. 264).}}}}
{{smaller block|But he refused, and said unto his master’s wife, Behold, my master ''wotteth'' not what is with me in the house.
{{right|Gen. xxxix. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|I ''wot'' well where he is. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 2. 139.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Nay, nay, God ''wot'', so thou wert nobly born,
Thou hast a pleasant presence.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}}}
(''b'') Preterit tense: I, etc., ''wist'' (erroneously ''wotted''). [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|Whanne she hadde seid thes thingis, she was turnyd a bak, and syȝ Jhesu stondinge, and ''wiste'' not for it was Jhesu.
{{right|''Wyclif'', John xx. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I whych ''woted'' best
His wretched dryftes.</poem>
{{right|''Sackville'', Complaint of Henry, Duke of Buckingham.}}}}
{{smaller block|He stood still, and ''wotted'' not what to do.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}
(''c'') Infinitive: ''wit'' (''to wit''); hence, ''to do to wit'', to cause (one) to know.
{{smaller block|For thoughe thou see me hidouse and horrible to loken onne, I ''do'' the ''to wytene'' that it is made be Enchauntement.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|And first it is to ''wyt'' that the Holy Londe, which was delyuered to the .xij. tribes of Israell, in parte it was called ye kyngdome of Jude.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 47.}}}}
{{smaller block|What wit haue we (poore fooles) to ''wit'' what wil serue vs?
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Cumfort against Tribulation (1573), fol. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|And his sister stood afar off to ''wit'' what would be done to him.
{{right|Ex. ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Moreover, brethren, we do you to ''wit'' of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia.
{{right|2 Cor. viii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now please you ''wit''
The epitaph is for Marina writ.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iv. 4. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|[The phrase ''to wit'' is now used chiefly to call attention to some particular, or as introductory to a detailed statement of what has been just before mentioned generally, and is equivalent to ‘namely,’ ‘that is to say’: as, there were three present—''to wit'', Mr. Brown, Mr. Green, and Mr. Black.}}

{{smaller block|Ius Ciuile was the order and manner in old dayes to forme their plees in lawe, that is ''to witt'' to cite, aunswere, accuse, proue, denie, alledge, relate, to giue sentence, and to execute.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 16.}}}}

{{smaller block|That which Moses saith, God built a woman, The Talmud interpreteth, He made curles, and he brought her to Adam, ''to wit'' with leaping and dancing.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 214.]}}}}

{{smaller block|(''d'') Present participle: ''witting'', sometimes ''weeting'' (erroneously ''wotting''). Compare ''unwitting''.}}
<poem>Yet are these feet . . .
Swift-winged with desire to get a grave,
As ''witting'' I no other comfort have.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 5. 16.}}}}

{{smaller block|(''e'') Past participle: ''wist''. [Obsolete or archaic.]}}
<poem>For harmes myghten folwen mo than two
If it were ''wist''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 615.}}}}
<poem>The grey border-stone that is ''wist''
To dilate and assume a wild shape in the mist.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Mrs. Browning'', Lay of the Brown Rosary.}}}}

'''wit<sup>1</sup>''' (wit), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wit'', ''wyt'' (pl. ''wittes''), < AS. ''wit'', knowledge, = OS. *''wit'' in comp. ''fire-wit'', curiosity, = OFries. ''wit'' = MLG. ''wite'', ''wete'' = OHG. ''wizzi'', MHG. ''witze'', G. ''witz'', knowledge, understanding, wisdom, = Icel. ''vit'' = Sw. ''vett'' = Dan. ''vid'', wit, knowledge; cf. Goth. ''un-wits'', without understanding, foolish, ''un-witi'', ignorance, foolishness; from the verb.]   '''1.''' Knowledge; wisdom; intelligence; sagacity; judgment; sense. {{smaller block|<poem>“It is but a Dido,” quod this doctour, “a dysoures tale.
Al the ''witt'' of this worlde and wiȝte mennes strengthe
Can nouȝt confourmen a pees bytwene the pope and his enemys.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiii. 172.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many things here among us have been found by chance, which no ''wit'' could ever have devised.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Had I but had the ''wit'' yestreen
That I hae coft the day—
I’d paid my kane seven times to hell
Ere you’d been won away!</poem>
{{right|''The Young Tamlane'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 125).}}}}
{{smaller block|I have the ''wit'' to think my master is a kind of a knave.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 262.}}}}
{{smaller block|If a man is honest, it detracts nothing from his merits to say he had the ''wit'' to see that honesty is the best policy.
{{right|''E. Dicey'', Victor Emmanuel, p. 112.}}}}
'''2.''' Mind; understanding; intellect; reason; in the plural, the faculties or powers of the mind or intellect; senses: as, to be out of one’s ''wits''; he has all his ''wits'' about him.
{{smaller block|<poem>So my ''witte'' wex and wanyed til I a fole were,
And somme lakked my lyf allowed it fewe,
And leten me for a lorel.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Who knew the ''wit'' of the Lord, or who was his counceilour?
{{right|''Wyclif'', Rom. xi. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many yong ''wittes'' be driuen to hate learninge before they know what learninge is.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|His ''wits'' are not so blunt.
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 5. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I am in my ''wits''; I am a labouring man,
And we have seldom leisure to run mad.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sir John Russel also was taken there, but he, feigning himself to be out of his ''Wits'', escaped for that Time.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 150.}}}}
'''3†.''' Knowledge; information. {{smaller block|<poem>The Child of Wynd got ''wit'' of it,
Which filled his heart with woe.</poem>
{{right|''The Laidley Worm of Spindleston-heugh'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 283).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let neither my father nor mother get ''wit'',
But that I’m coming hame.</poem>
{{right|''The Queen’s Marie'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 119).}}}}
'''4.''' Ingenuity; skill.
{{smaller block|<poem>Your knyf withe alle your ''wytte''
Vnto youre sylf bothe clene and sharpe conserve,
That honestly yee mowe your own mete kerve.</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|What strength cannot do, man’s ''wit'' — being the most forcible engine — hath often effected.
{{right|''Raleigh'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 16).}}}}
'''5.''' Imagination; the imaginative faculty. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Wit'' in the poet . . . is no other than the faculty of imagination in the writer, which . . . searches over all the memory for the species or ideas of those things which it designs to represent.
{{right|''Dryden'', Annus Mirabilis, To Sir R. Howard.}}}}
'''6.''' The keen perception and apt expression of those connections between ideas which awaken pleasure and especially amusement. See the quotations and the synonyms.
{{smaller block|True ''wit'' consists in the resemblance of ideas. . . . But every resemblance of ideas is not what we call ''wit'', and it must be such an one that gives delight and surprise to the reader. Where the likeness is obvious, it creates no surprise, and is not ''wit''. Thus, when a poet tells us that the bosom of his mistress is as white as snow, there is no ''wit'' in the comparison; but when he adds, with a sigh, it is as cold too, it then grows into ''wit''.
{{right|''Addison''.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Wit'' lying most in the assemblage of ideas, and putting those together with quickness and variety wherein can be found any resemblance or congruity, thereby to make up pleasant pictures and agreeable visions in the fancy.
{{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, II. xi. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|In ''wit'', if by ''wit'' be meant the power of perceiving analogies between things which appear to have nothing in common, he never had an equal. {{right|''Macaulay'', Bacon.}}}}

'''7†.''' Conceit; idea; thought; design; scheme; plan.
{{smaller block|<poem>To senden him into som fer contree
Ther as this Jasoun may destroyed be;
This was his ''wit''. ''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 1420.</poem>}}

{{smaller block|Was ’t not a pretty ''wit'' of mine, master poet, to have had him rode into Puckeridge with a horn before him?
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, v. 1.}}}}

'''At one’s wit’s end.''' See ''end''.—'''Kind wit†.''' See ''kind''<sup>1</sup>.—'''The five wits''', the five senses; in general, the faculties of the mind. The five wits have been fancifully enumerated as common wit, imagination, fantasy, estimation, memory.

{{smaller block|The deedly synnes that been entred into thyn herte by thy ''five wittes''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Tale of Melibeus.}}}}

{{smaller block|If thy ''wits'' run the wild-goose chase, I have done, for thou hast more of the wild-goose in one of thy ''wits'' than . . . I have in my whole ''five''. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4. 77, 78.}}}}

<poem>Alone and warming his ''five wits'',
The white owl in the belfry sits.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', The Owl.}}}}

'''To drive to one’s wit’s end.''' See ''drive''.—'''To have one’s wits in a creel.''' See ''creel''.—'''To live by one’s wits''', to live by temporary shifts or expedients, as one without regular means of living.

{{smaller block|Addison sent to beg Gay, who was then ''living by his wits'' about town, to come to Holland House.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Addison.}}}}

='''Syn. 6.''' ''Wit, Humor.'' In writers down to the time of Pope ''wit'' generally meant the serious kind of ''wit''.

{{smaller block|Serious ''wit'' is . . . neither more nor less than quick wisdom.
{{right|''Burnet.''}}}}

{{smaller block|Look, he’s winding up the watch of his ''wit''; by and by it will strike.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 1. 13.}}}}

{{smaller block|In more recent use ''wit'' in the singular generally implies comic ''wit''; in that sense it is different from ''humor.'' One principal difference is that ''wit'' always lies in some form of words, while ''humor'' may be expressed by manner, as a smile, a grimace, an attitude. Underlying this is the fact, consistent with the original meaning of the words, that ''humor'' goes more deeply into the nature of the thought, while ''wit'' catches pleasing but occult or far-fetched resemblances between things really unlike: a good pun shows ''wit;'' Irving’s “History of New York” is a piece of sustained ''humor'', the ''humor'' lying in the portrayal of character, the nature of the incidents, etc. Again, “''Wit'' may, I think, be regarded as a purely intellectual process, while ''humor'' is a sense of the ridiculous controlled by feeling, and coexistent often with the gentlest and deepest pathos” (''H. Reed'', Lects. on Eng. Lit., xi. 357). Hence ''humor'' is always kind, while ''wit'' may be unkind in the extreme: Swift’s “Travels of Gulliver” is much too severe a satire to be called a work of ''humor.'' It is essential to the effect of ''wit'' that the form in which it is expressed should be brief; ''humor'' may be heightened in its effect by expansion into full forms of statement, description, etc. ''Wit'' more often than ''humor'' depends upon passing circumstances for its effect.}}

{{smaller block|The best and most agreeable specimen of English ''humor'' (it is ''humor'' in contrast to ''wit'') which belongs to that period is Steele’s invention, and Addison’s use, of the character of Sir Roger de Coverley. . . . The same species of pure, genial, wise, and healthful ''humor'' has been sustained in the incomparable “Vicar of Wakefield,” and in the writings of our countryman Washington Irving.
{{right|''H. Reed'', Lects. on Eng. Lit., xi. 369.}}}}

{{smaller block|While ''wit'' is a purely intellectual thing, into every act of the humorous mind there is an influx of the moral nature; rays, direct or refracted, from the will and the affections, from the disposition and the temperament, enter into all ''humor;'' and thence it is that ''humor'' is of a diffusive quality, pervading an entire course of thought; while ''wit'' — because it has no existence apart from certain logical relations of thought which are definitely assignable, and can be counted even — is always punctually concentrated within the circle of a few words. {{right|''De Quincey.''}}}}

{{smaller block|Dr. Trusler says that ''wit'' relates to the matter, ''humour'' to the manner; that our old comedies abounded with ''wit,'' and our old actors with ''humour;'' that ''humour'' always excites laughter but ''wit'' does not; that a fellow of ''humour'' will set a whole company in a roar, but that there is a smartness in ''wit'' which cuts while it pleases. ''Wit,'' he adds, always implies sense and abilities, while ''humour'' does not; ''humour'' is chiefly relished by the vulgar, but education is requisite to comprehend ''wit.''
{{right|''Fleming,'' Vocab. Philos.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is no uncommon thing to hear “He has ''humour'' rather than ''wit.''” Here the expression commonly means pleasantry; for whoever has ''humour'' has ''wit,'' although it does not follow that whoever has ''wit'' has ''humour. Humour'' is ''wit'' appertaining to character, and indulges in breadth of drollery rather than in play and brilliancy of point. ''Wit'' vibrates and spirts; ''humour'' springs up exuberantly as from a fountain and runs on. In Congreve you wonder what he will say next; in Addison you repose on what is said, listening with assured expectation of something congenial and pertinent. {{right|''Landor.''}}}}

<poem>Small room for Fancy’s many chorded lyre,
For ''Wit’s'' bright rockets with their trains of fire.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''O. W. Holmes,'' An After-Dinner Poem.}}}}

{{smaller block|I am not speaking of the fun of the book [Don Quixote], of which there is plenty, and sometimes boisterous enough, but of that deeper and more delicate quality, suggestive of remote analogies and essential incongruities, which alone deserves the name of ''humor.'' {{right|''Lowell,'' Don Quixote.}}}}

'''wit'''<sup>2</sup> (wit), ''n.''   [Prob. another use, and certainly now regarded as another use, of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''; cf. ''spirit'', a person of lively mind or energy, from ''spirit'', liveliness, energy; ''witness'', a person who has knowledge, from ''witness'', knowledge. But ''wit'' as applied to a person may in part represent, as it may phonetically descend from, the ME. *''wit'', ''wet'', ''wite'', ''weote'', < AS. ''wita'', ''weota'', also ''gewita'', a man of knowledge, an adviser, counselor, = OF. ''wita'', a witness, = OHG. ''wizo'', a witness; lit. ‘one who knows,’ with formative ''a''- (''-an'') of agent, < ''witan'', know: see ''wit''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' This AS. ''wita'' appears in the historical term ''witenagemot'', AS. ''witena gemōt'', ‘wits’ moot, moot of counselors,’ a council, parliament.]   One who has discernment, reason, or judgment; a person of acute perception; especially, one who detects between associated ideas the finer resemblances or contrasts which give pleasure or enjoyment to the mind, and who gives expression to these for the entertainment of others; often, a person who has a keen perception of the incongruous or ludicrous, and uses it for the amusement and frequently at the expense of others.
{{smaller block|By providing that choice ''wits'' after reasonable time spent in contemplation may at the length either enter into that holy vocation . . . or else give place and suffer others to succeed in their rooms.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O, sure I am, the ''wits'' of former days
To subjects worse have given admiring praise.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lix.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When I die,</poem> I’ll build an almshouse for decayèd ''wits.''
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, v. 2.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
